statements.sources: First sentence: two independent New Zealand voices support it in full (NZRS-FAQ; Auckland Botanic Gardens through ABG-R, NZRS-ABG and SIBB, one body of experience per ARC 8.1). UCIPM-DIS, UCIPM-INS and ZLESAK are marked 'partly': UC speaks of fungicides ('especially in California's dry interior valleys') and of insecticides on separate pages, and ZLESAK 'describes how the trials are run; it does not itself say roses grow well without spraying'. Second sentence: NZRS-FAQ ('Grow varieties that are very disease tolerant'), ABG-R ('We only grow those that perform well and stay healthy without spraying') and SIBB ('Suitable cultivars are chosen for public display') tie it to variety choice. NZRS-ABG's sentence does not: it ties it to 'roses mixed in with other garden plants including New Zealand natives'. 'Disease tolerant' is the Rose Society's word only.
statements.wording: The second sentence is not in AF-1's wording. 'The New Zealand sources' reads as all four; three of the four recorded quotations support it. Limit line matches ARC 4A. 'The University of California says it especially of dry climates': the page says it of fungicides only and of 'California's dry interior valleys'.
statements.rules: ok. High finding; limits are given anyway.
statements.note: Stands. To know: (1) 'The New Zealand sources tie this to growing disease-tolerant varieties' is true of the Rose Society FAQ, the Botanic Gardens' page and the published account, but not of the Rose Society's page about the Gardens, whose sentence ties no spraying to mixed planting. (2) The University of California's sentence is about fungicides, in California's dry interior valleys. Wording fully supported: 'The New Zealand Rose Society ties this to growing very disease-tolerant varieties, and Auckland Botanic Gardens grows only varieties that stay healthy without spraying.'

statements.sources: Six pages from five voices recommend choosing resistant or tolerant varieties in so many words (NZRS-FAQ, TRE-BS, UCIPM-BS, UMD-BS, UMD-PROB, WISC-BS). No page ranks it as a 'main' or 'principal' way; the nearest is UMD-PROB '(very important!)'. Seven entries are 'partly' (GU-DIS, RNZIH, RHS-PM, RHS-RUST, CLEM-DIS, ZLESAK): they say cultivars differ, not that choosing them is a principal control.
statements.wording: Matches ARC 6.1 ('a main way to reduce disease'). The ranking word is the ARC's, not any source's. Most sources say 'resistant'; 'tolerant' is the NZ Rose Society's word.
statements.note: Stands on the approved finding. To know: 'a main way' is the record's summary; no confirmed page ranks variety choice against other measures, and one calls it 'very important'. Wording the pages support without the ranking: 'Sources say to choose disease-resistant or disease-tolerant varieties to reduce disease.'

statements.sources: RHS-BS: 'Gardeners may gain a few years' respite by planting the newest cultivars which claim resistance, but ... this usually does not last' - said of the newest cultivars and of black spot. RHS-PM says only that claimed resistance 'may not persist for the lifetime of the plant, or be effective in all localities'. UMD-BS: 'resistance can be regionally variable' (regional only). Auckland: SIBB abstract confirmed as 'Miticides, insecticides and fungicides are not used' and 'Suitable cultivars are chosen'; 'for two decades' comes from ARC C-3 ('SIBB over two decades in Auckland') and the article title (2000-2020), and was not itself among the wording reopened.

statements.rules: C-3 is recorded as an unresolved conflict. The statement is not marked kind 'disagreement' (package 13 says disagreements are all marked the same way). statements.note: Stands. Wording fully supported: 'The RHS says the resistance claimed for the newest varieties usually doesn't last. ... Against that, Auckland Botanic Gardens' published account of 2000 to 2020 describes growing chosen varieties without spraying.'

statements.sources: Harm: CLEM-INS says 'these insecticides kill the natural enemies of rose aphids', where 'these' are 'Higher toxicity insecticides'; UCIPM-INS says 'Soil-applied systemic insecticides ... may harm pollinators and natural enemies' and that spider mites' natural enemies 'are killed by broad-spectrum insecticides'. Repeat outbreaks: UMD-PROB ('choose control measures that minimize impacts on natural enemies, or else secondary (recurring) pest outbreaks can be problematic' - 'control measures' generally, no insecticide class named); UCIPM-INS (spider mite numbers 'may greatly increase'). CLEM-INS 'does not state repeat outbreaks in so many words'.
statements.wording: 'Harm' now matches the finding. Dropping 'broad-spectrum' leaves 'insecticides' with no qualifier, which is a wider class than the finding names and wider than any page: each page that names a class qualifies it ('Higher toxicity', 'broad-spectrum', 'Soil-applied systemic'). 'Can harm' keeps the sentence true, but it now sits beside item 2, where the same record says soaps and oils have 'only moderate impact'.
statements.note: Stands; the first-check fault ('kill') is corrected. To know: taking out 'broad-spectrum' made the statement about insecticides in general. No source says that: Clemson says it of 'higher toxicity insecticides', the University of California of 'broad-spectrum' and 'soil-applied systemic' insecticides, and the University of Maryland speaks of 'control measures'. Wording the pages support: 'Sources say stronger insecticides can harm aphids' natural enemies. The University of Maryland says harming natural enemies can lead to repeat pest outbreaks.' Or name each source for the kind it names.

package.coverage: All 41 findings Available to Pip in ARC 3 are used by at least one statement except AF-26 (checked by counting the traces). AF-26 is listed in package 1 as held, with the reason, which ARC 7 item 2 allows. On the holding: the source notes confirm the fact the builder relies on - GA-LOOK and TRE-BS state the full order (clear up, then spray the plant and the ground), and SPR supports only 'Prune roses first' ('The page does NOT mention clearing prunings or leaves first, or spraying the ground'). I agree holding is justified while the finding's wording and rating are open. Two things the notes do not settle: (1) the notes do not force a hold - a statement naming the two sources that do say it ('ABC Gardening Australia and Treloar Roses say to clear prunings and fallen leaves first, then spray the plant and the ground around it') would be fully supported and would say less than the finding, the same treatment the builder gave AF-4, AF-33 and AF-36; (2) whether two sources make the finding Low is a rating decision under the Evidence Assessment Standard, not something the source notes show. Both remaining sources are Australian; no New Zealand source says it. While it is held, gardeners in New Zealand and Australia are not told to clear up before a winter spray or that sources spray the ground.
package.misuse: None found. No statement traces to AF-13, AF-27, AF-35, AF-43 or R-5, and no statement's wording uses their content: no purpose is given for the winter spray (AF-27), nothing on copper washing off (AF-43), nothing on whether frequent spraying is justified (AF-13), and the pointer to a rose society at PKR-CGD-000009 item 8 comes from R-3 and rule 5, not AF-35. AF-29 is used only to say the gap. Place and kind conditions are met on every statement: AF-25, AF-36, AF-37 and AF-38 statements have place exactly NZ, AU; the AF-45 statement has place exactly US and says only one source was found; every AF-28, AF-31, AF-33, AF-41 and AF-42 statement has kind 'precaution'.
package.gaps: R-1: said at PKR-CGD-000014 item 2 and PKR-CGD-000011 item 3 (everyone). R-2: PKR-CGD-000013 item 7 (New Zealand and Australia). R-3: PKR-CGD-000009 item 8 (New Zealand). R-4: PKR-CGD-000012 item 7 (New Zealand). All four are said. Only the R-3 statement points the gardener to local expert help; rule 5 asks for that pointer with every gap.
package.conflicts: C-1: yes (PKR-CGD-000009 items 6 and 7). C-2: yes (PKR-CGD-000012 item 2). C-3: yes (PKR-CGD-000009 item 3), though not marked as a disagreement. C-4: yes, if PKR-CGD-000010 items 5 and 6 are both seen; item 5 alone gives no hint of the powdery mildew exception. C-5: gardeners in New Zealand and Australia, yes (PKR-CGD-000013 items 1 to 8). Gardeners in the UK and the US, and any gardener whose place is not known, see only item 8 (and, in the US, item 9): they learn that UK and US institutional pages don't describe a spray after pruning, but not that New Zealand and Australian sources describe one. That follows ARC 7 item 3 and rule 4; it means they see one side of C-5. C-6: partly. A gardener learns that sources put copper on at different times (PKR-CGD-000013 item 3), that oil goes on with copper or later (item 4), and the two precautions (items 5 and 6). No statement says that sources differ on the order of the winter sprays, and no timing is given for lime sulphur. AF-28, which carries the order, is Low and available only as a precaution, so this is the most the record allows. C-7: yes, as a range (PKR-CGD-000012 item 5). C-8: yes (PKR-CGD-000011 item 4).
package.first_check: AF-4 (PKR-CGD-000009 item 4): passes. It now names the RHS and its black spot page, says 'One source', and the wording is the RHS's own sentence. AF-8 (PKR-CGD-000010 item 1): passes, with a note. 'Most commonly occurring' is now attributed to the Rose Society of NSW and the limit says only one source says it. The remaining point is 'needs': one page says leaves 'must remain wet', the other that wet leaves 'encourage' infection. AF-23 (PKR-CGD-000015 item 2): passes. The 'only moderate' effect is now given to the University of California alone, and Clemson and Ross Roses are named only for soap sprays. AF-24 (PKR-CGD-000015 item 3): passes, with a note. 'Kill' is now 'harm'. But removing 'broad-spectrum' left 'insecticides' unqualified, which is wider than the finding and than any page; every source that names a class qualifies it.

corrections.AF-4: Yes. Notes: RHS-BS supports susceptibility only and itself recommends against fungicides; ARS-FUNG says 'some application', not regular; UMD-BS says 'Most people' and does not limit itself to susceptible roses, Hybrid Teas or Floribundas; RSNSW 'does not mention fungicide specifically ... or susceptibility'. No page says susceptible roses need regular fungicide to stay healthy.
corrections.AF-7: Yes. ARS-FUNG says 'most fungicides', that 'only a handful are effective against pathogens once infection occurs', and names a curative fungicide; UCIPM-DIS says 'generally'; RSNSW says spraying will 'slow down the disease'; the notes on SPR, UMD-BS, WISC-BS and PSU-RD say those pages do not state that fungicides cannot cure.
corrections.AF-8: Yes. Only RSNSW says 'most commonly occurring'; GU-DIS 'lists four main diseases without ranking'; UCIPM-BS says black spot 'is usually a problem in California only in foggy or humid coastal areas'. (ARC 4A already records this as a limitation.)
corrections.AF-21: Yes. Potassium bicarbonate is on the UC pages only; Clemson names 'baking soda (sodium bicarbonate), not potassium bicarbonate', under powdery mildew only and in a list with synthetic fungicides. No recorded quotation says 'lower-toxicity', and the Clemson note says it 'does not call these lower-toxicity in this sentence'; the notes do not record a search of the whole of each page for that idea, so that part is shown for the quotations, not for the pages.
corrections.AF-24: Partly. The notes support the claim that one source uses 'broad-spectrum': CLEM-INS and UMD-PROB do not use the words. But the proposed wording, 'Insecticides can harm natural enemies', is not what the sources say either: Clemson says it of 'Higher toxicity insecticides', UC of 'broad-spectrum' and 'Soil-applied systemic' insecticides, and Maryland of 'control measures'. The notes also show CLEM-INS does not state repeat outbreaks, and that the UCIPM-INS quotation on record is about soil-applied systemic insecticides. A correction should keep a qualifier.
corrections.AF-26: Partly. Yes on the fact: SPR supports only spraying after pruning, and two sources (GA-LOOK, TRE-BS) state the rest. The proposed new rating (Low; on record only) is a judgement under the Evidence Assessment Standard that the source notes do not decide.
corrections.AF-33: Yes. ROSS-SP: 'the 25-degree limit is stated only for the winter copper / lime sulphur sprays after pruning. The page says nothing else about temperature, hot weather or time of day.' TRE-BS says 'Never in the heat of the day', of growing-season spraying.
corrections.AF-36: Yes. TUI: 'after pruning is not on the page'. SPR: copper 'at first spring growth, on its own, not straight after pruning and not together with oil'. NZRS-W and ROSS-SP put it on after pruning. 'Often with a spraying oil' is two of the four (NZRS-W, TUI).

other: One statement fails: PKR-CGD-000012 item 5, second sentence. The source note shows the two-to-three-week regime in SIBB was 'recommended by ABG for a home gardener', not the Gardens' own programme. ARC AF-10 ('Auckland Botanic Gardens' former programme') and C-7 ('formerly sprayed') carry the same wording. This is a ninth correction to the research record that package 14 does not list.

Two attributions rest on quotations in ARC 4 that are not in the Source Register and that the source check did not reopen: the RHS's 'may favour other diseases' (PKR-CGD-000010 item 6) and the New Zealand EPA's 'when bees are foraging' (PKR-CGD-000014 item 3). 'For two decades' (PKR-CGD-000009 item 3) is in the same position. All 187 checked quotations were confirmed, but these three were not among them. They should be confirmed on the pages before publishing.

Rule 5 asks Pip to point the gardener to local expert help wherever it says no source was found. Only PKR-CGD-000009 item 8 does. PKR-CGD-000012 item 7 and PKR-CGD-000013 items 7 and 8 do not. The ARC's 'Until then' wording for R-2 and R-4 does not ask for it, so this may need a Founder's ruling on whether the rule applies to each gap statement.

Other places where the source notes show the ARC's wording is stronger than the pages, not listed in package 14: AF-2 'a principal way' (no page ranks it); AF-8 'depends on leaves staying wet' (one page says 'must', one 'encourage'); AF-11 (Wisconsin's two conditions are joined by 'and' and concern whether to spray preventively; each condition has one source); AF-17 'watering at the base' (one source); AF-22 squashing (one source); AF-37 'after pruning' and 'New Zealand and Australian rose sources' (NZRS-W does not say lime sulphur goes on after pruning; EUTREMA is a UK company). The statements for AF-37 already avoid the last.

Package 14's list of findings needing limitations added leaves out AF-14, AF-19, AF-20, AF-28 and AF-29, each of which has a 'partly' entry in the source check (ABG-R twice, NZRS-FAQ, EUTREMA, CLEM-DIS), and includes AF-18, whose three entries are all 'yes'.

Source Register: the SIBB quotation for AF-10 is 'NOT on the listed URL'; it is in the article's PDF. The register's web address or note needs correcting, alongside the ABC date the package already lists.

Limit lines are uneven for the winter-spray findings. ARC 4A gives AF-36 and AF-37 the limitation 'no source measures the effect', and AF-36 'the NZ Rose Society article dates from 1996'. PKR-CGD-000013 item 2 omits the first and item 3 omits the second.

Sources are not always identified well enough for a statement read on its own (rule 1, who says it). 'The RHS' is never spelled out, and is described as a UK body only at PKR-CGD-000009 item 7. Ross Roses and Treloar Roses are Australian nurseries; no statement says where they are, and PKR-CGD-000012 item 2 and PKR-CGD-000014 item 4 name Ross Roses with no description at all. South Pacific Roses, by contrast, is described as 'a New Zealand rose nursery'.

The confidence chip is the finding's level, and several statements use only part of a finding. PKR-CGD-000009 item 4 shows 'Moderate confidence' on one source's sentence. PKR-CGD-000012 item 7 and PKR-CGD-000013 item 8 show 'No source found' over a sentence that is a positive claim from Moderate and Very High findings. PKR-CGD-000009 item 3 shows 'Moderate confidence' over a sentence from a High finding (AF-1). None breaks the stated convention; a reader of the chip should know it.

Where a gardener's place is not known, the answer to 'What about a winter spray after pruning?' is only PKR-CGD-000013 item 8 and the label reminder: a statement about UK and US pages, with nothing on what New Zealand and Australian sources say. That follows ARC 7 item 3. The Founders may want to see that rendering before approving.

The record treats the same Ross Roses sentence ('Spraying of roses should only occur minimally and when the problems are really bad') as support for the better-supported view in C-1 (AF-6, High) and as one side of an evenly split C-2. A gardener reading PKR-CGD-000009 item 6 and PKR-CGD-000012 item 2 together is told that minimal spraying is the better-supported view and also that neither view is better supported. Both statements follow ARC 6.1; the tension is in the record.
PKR-CGD-000014 item 5 gives '25 degrees' with no unit to gardeners in every country, including the United States.

Precautions that bear on winter spraying are not all in the winter answer: AF-33 (Ross Roses' temperature limit, stated for winter sprays) and AF-42 (no oil within two weeks of a sulfur spray) appear only under 'How do I spray safely?' and, for AF-42, under the sprays question. The winter answer reaches them through its closing reminder. Rule 7 says Pip always includes a precaution where sources give one.
Package 1 lists PKR-CGD-000014 item 2 twice in the R-1 row. No effect on the count.

Checked and clean across all 55: first person throughout; no 'he'; no product brand (companies appear only as sources; active ingredients and spray types only); no mixing amount or recipe; no months; every confidence value equals the ARC 3 level of the first finding in its trace.
